title: Rerun the one-edit study per edit kind with shuffled slots against the full meta
headline: Swapping one whole Pokemon moves a team further than one step moves a standard benchmark
setup: A team is six Pokemon, listed in six slots. The meta is the 50 highest-placing team files, one team listed twice. We change one thing on a team, battle the old and the new team against the meta, and see how far the win rate moves. September's battles used rules the project no longer counts, so the study ran again.
alt: Eight frames. The rerun battled every team against all 50 meta files with the six Pokemon shuffled before each battle. An edit changes one thing on one Pokemon, in one of six kinds, and each kind is tried 3 times on a team. Replays of the unchanged team show battle noise, about 3.40 points. With noise removed, one edit moves win rate by 5.90 points for a whole Pokemon swap, 4.84 for a move, 4.35 for an item, 3.66 for an ability, 1.95 for stat alignment and 1.60 for Stat Points. No size cutoff is used. Four kinds have a 95% interval above zero from tournament-ready teams, and the two Stat kinds do not. As a share of the 9.04-point spread between teams, the whole Pokemon swap is 0.65, larger than one step on the Pest Control benchmark, which is 0.37 of the spread between its random starting points and 0.32 between its hill-climbed ones. Move, item and ability edits are undecided against that step. From search-found teams only the whole Pokemon swap and the move edit are above zero.
terms: Edit kind
What one rule-abiding edit changes on one Pokemon. Four kinds pick a new legal value at random: one of its four moves, its ability, the item it holds, its stat alignment
Copied edits

The other two kinds copy from real teams. Stat Points: all six numbers are replaced by those of another real set of the same species. Whole Pokemon: the slot is replaced by a real set of a species not on the team, with its moves, item, ability, stat alignment and Stat Points
Stat alignment, Stat Points
Two settings of a Pokemon's numbers: which stat is raised and which lowered, and how its training points are divided among its stats
Shuffled slots
The six Pokemon get a new random order before every battle. The battle policy picks by position, so a fixed order biases scores
Replay
The same team battled 384 more times with nothing changed. Every starting team gets 3 replays
Battle noise
How far a win rate moves on a replay, by luck alone. Here a replay typically moves a score by 3.40 points
Change, in points

The size of the real move one edit causes, in win-rate percentage points, in either direction. Computed as the square root of the mean squared move after an edit minus the mean squared move of a replay, because independent parts add as squares
95% interval
The range the true size plausibly lies in. Found by redrawing the starting teams 2,000 times and recomputing the size each time
Above zero
Reading 1. The whole interval of an edit kind's size sits above zero, so the edit does something a replay does not. It says the edit is real, not how large
Spread between teams
How far the starting teams' true win rates lie from one another, as a standard deviation with battle noise removed: 9.04 points
Share of the spread
An edit's size divided by the spread between teams. A share of 0.65 means one edit moves a team by 0.65 of one standard deviation of team scores
One Pest Control step

Reading 2. Pest Control is a standard optimisation benchmark. One step on it is 0.37 of the spread between its random starting points and 0.32 between its hill-climbed ones. The two kinds of starting point are not pooled, because their average scores differ and that gap would make the step look small. An edit kind is larger when the interval of its share minus the step's share sits above zero for both, and undecided when that interval includes zero
The dropped 5-point line
The plan of 2026-09-28 also required a change of at least 5 points and gave no reason for the number. The owner removed it on 2026-11-13, after the result. Under it only the whole Pokemon swap passed
Tournament-ready teams, search-found teams
The two groups of starting teams: 24 real teams players built for tournaments, drawn from outside the top 50, and 16 teams an earlier search produced

frames.title: 1. Why the study ran again

left.title: September study
lines: 36 of the 50 meta files as opponents

frames.takes: The rerun fixes the opponents and the slot order, and changes nothing else on purpose.
frames.measured: Two things changed that were not planned. The 24 tournament-ready starting teams are a fresh draw, 2 shared with September, so the two runs are not paired. And the reading in frames 6 to 8 was chosen after the result.

frames.title: 2. The six kinds of edit, on one real team

rows.label: Stat Points, copied
rows.after: Another real Raichu's set: HP 32, Speed 24, Defense 10

rows.label: Whole Pokemon, copied
rows.after: A real Mawile set from another team

frames.takes: Four kinds pick a new legal value at random. Two kinds copy from real teams: Stat Points from another set of the same species, and a whole Pokemon of a new species.
frames.measured: These are real edits from the run, each on one Pokemon with the other five left alone. The team is Raichu, Staraptor, Garchomp, Charizard, Gholdengo and Sylveon.

frames.title: 3. Three different edits of each kind
frames.takes: Each kind is tried 3 times on a team, each time with a different change, so one lucky pick cannot decide the result.
frames.measured: These are the same team's three move edits. 6 kinds times 3 edits is 18 edited teams for each starting team, and 720 across the 40 starting teams.

frames.title: 4. A replay: the same team, battled again

right.title: A replay
lines: Battle the same team 384 more times

frames.takes: A replay shows how far a score moves by luck alone. That move is battle noise.
frames.measured: The team in frame 2 scored 56.25%, then 52.3%, 53.1% and 52.9% on its 3 replays. A typical replay moves a score by 3.40 points.

frames.title: 5. From scores to a change in points

hypotenuse.label: What we measure after an edit

frames.takes: What we measure after an edit is its real move plus battle noise. The two are independent, so they add as squares, like the short sides of a right triangle.
frames.measured: For the whole Pokemon swap: 6.81 squared minus 3.40 squared is 5.90 squared. Plain subtraction would give 3.41 and undercount the edit.

frames.title: 6. Is the edit real? Change in points with its 95% interval, tournament-ready teams
frames.takes: An edit kind is real when its whole interval, the thin capped line, sits above zero. Four kinds are. Stat alignment and Stat Points reach zero, so no effect is shown for them, which is not proof they do nothing.
frames.measured: The whole Pokemon swap is 5.90 points, interval 4.78 to 7.01. From search-found teams only the whole Pokemon swap, 5.85, and the move edit, 4.92, stay above zero.

frames.title: 7. Is the edit large? Its share of the spread between teams, against one step on a benchmark
frames.takes: The yardstick is a benchmark, not a number someone picked. Each size is divided by how far teams' scores spread, 9.04 points. One step on Pest Control is 0.37 of the spread between its random starting points, and 0.32 between its hill-climbed ones.
frames.measured: A whole Pokemon swap is 0.65 of the spread, and its interval clears the step. Move, item and ability edits sit above the step, but their intervals reach it, so they are undecided.

frames.title: 8. The two readings, kind by kind

cols: Larger than a Pest Control step

frames.takes: Two kinds are real from both groups of teams: the whole Pokemon swap and the move edit. Only the whole Pokemon swap is shown larger than the benchmark's step, and only from tournament-ready teams.
frames.measured: Corrected 2026-11-13: an earlier version pooled the benchmark's two kinds of starting point, which made its step 0.14 and four kinds larger. The plan of 2026-09-28 also required a change of at least 5 points, with no reason for the number. That line was removed after the result, so this frame is a reading made afterwards.
